title: Sing a new song (Psalm 96)
hookLine: let the fields be joyful and the trees sing
tomorrow: bless the Lord, O my soul
last: WARM AND DARK AND LOUD WITH HEARTBEATS.

lines: WHEN DID YOU LAST SING SOMETHING NEW?
cards: When did you last sing something for the first time? Not the chorus stuck in your head since the drive to work. Not the birthday song, or the hymn you could sing in your sleep.
Something new in your own mouth. For most adults, it's been years, and there's comfort in the familiar. But the Psalms keep asking for something else.
Again and again: sing a new song. And Psalm ninety-six doesn't stop at people. By the end, the fields, the sea and the trees are singing too.

teach.h: NEW SONG, FROM PSALMS TO REVELATION
teach.b: Psalm ninety-six opens, in the King James Bible: "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth."

That phrase, a new song, turns up in several psalms, in the prophet Isaiah, and then twice in Revelation, the Bible's last book, where it's still being called new. So new here doesn't mean the latest hit.
In the Psalms, a new song usually answers something new God has done: a rescue, a victory, a homecoming.
Fresh mercy deserves fresh words. And this new song isn't for one nation. All the earth.
The psalm tells the families of the peoples to give glory, and it says the gods of the nations are idols, but the Lord made the heavens. Then the song spreads beyond people altogether.

"Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad; let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof. Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice." Why are the trees so happy?
The last verse says: "For he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth." That sounds alarming, but listen to how it ends: "he shall judge the world with righteousness, and the people with his truth."
In the Psalms, judgment often means setting things right. The trees cheer because justice is finally coming. And this psalm has a second home.

teach.h: O SING UNTO THE LORD A NEW SONG.
teach.b: Most of it appears again in First Chronicles, in the song sung when David brought the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem.

how: Psalm 96 is sung in many churches at Christmas and other feasts, and Christians often take its call to "sing a new song" as a reason to write new hymns and worship music for each generation.

o: old, as in the old songs
new, as in a new song

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: answers something new God has done

s: the phrase a new song appears only once in the Bible
it appears in several psalms, in Isaiah, and twice in Revelation.
in Psalm 96, the trees of the wood rejoice
verse 12: "then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice."
in this psalm, God coming to judge is bad news for the earth
the whole earth sings because he will judge "with righteousness": things set right.

games.q: the psalm says the Lord is coming to judge the earth. you're a tree in the field. how does the psalm say you respond?
games.why: "then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice before the LORD: for he cometh." in the Psalms, judgment often means justice at last.

practice: Take the psalm's first line, O sing unto the Lord a new song, and give it a tune that didn't exist a minute ago: hum it first, then try the words; three notes, off key, it doesn't matter.
If you'd rather, sing a hymn or a song you've never sung aloud before. If you pray, let it be your prayer; if you don't, let it be a small act of courage, and rest in the quiet after.

wordCard.voice: Chadash. Hebrew for new, the word behind Psalm ninety-six's call to sing a new song, with fresh words for fresh mercy, the fields and trees joining in.

orig.note: Hebrew: a new song. chadash, new, is the same word Ezekiel uses for a new heart.

carryVoice: Your line: a new song. Even the trees get a part. That's day four hundred thirty.
